bullets: How cells release energy from glucose in respiration, rebuild ATP, and how photosynthesis in chloroplasts builds glucose in the first place
slides.heading: JC H2 biology — energetics: respiration and photosynthesis
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we link respiration and photosynthesis through energy - mitochondria and cristae, the ATP cycle, anaerobic pathways, photolysis and the Calvin cycle, and limiting factors.

bullets: Describe aerobic respiration and the ATP-ADP cycle, including why cristae give mitochondria a huge surface area
Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast and in muscle, and state the products of each pathway
Explain photolysis and the Calvin cycle, and judge photosynthesis claims using limiting factors
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including correcting the respiration trap.

bullets: A green plant photosynthesises in bright light all day, then sits in darkness overnight
Is its respiration switched off in the light, on only at night, or running the whole time?
slides.heading: A plant in the dark: is it still respiring?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any definitions: night only, day only, or around the clock? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because scene s2 settles this exactly.

bullets: Respiration transfers energy from glucose to ATP, and ATP hydrolysis releases that energy where the cell needs it
Photosynthesis does the reverse build: light energy drives photolysis and the Calvin cycle to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water
slides.heading: One idea, six scenes: energy is transferred, never created
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea: glucose is not spent directly - ATP is the energy currency, and photosynthesis and respiration are linked through glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water.

bullets: The inner mitochondrial membrane folds into cristae, packing a huge surface area into a tiny space for respiratory enzymes
More surface area means more ATP can be made by aerobic respiration
slides.heading: Mitochondria: folded cristae, huge surface area
slides.notes: Narrate the folding: watch the cristae grow and the energy dot travel the folded path. Say: folding means huge surface area, so more ATP is made.

bullets: The trap claim in full: Plants only respire at night. It feels true because photosynthesis dominates by day - but the evidence in this scene says otherwise
Aerobic respiration runs around the clock: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy, releasing about 32 ATP per glucose
slides.heading: A common mistake: plants only respire at night
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud: Plants only respire at night. Then land the correction: Plants respire around the clock: at night there is simply no photosynthesis to hide it.

bullets: ATP hydrolysis splits off a phosphate and releases usable energy, leaving ADP
Respiration rebuilds ATP in the mitochondrion: ADP picks up a phosphate and becomes ATP again
slides.heading: ATP hydrolysis releases energy; respiration rebuilds ATP
slides.notes: Follow the cycle: ATP to ADP at the work site, then ADP back to the mitochondrion to be recharged. Say: ATP is the energy currency - cells spend ATP, never glucose directly.

bullets: Without enough oxygen, glucose is only partly broken down: yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide
Muscle makes lactic acid instead - and both anaerobic pathways yield far less ATP than aerobic respiration
slides.heading: Anaerobic: yeast → ethanol + CO₂; muscle → lactic acid
slides.notes: Follow the fork from one glucose down two paths. Stress the catch shown in the scene: far less ATP than aerobic, because glucose is only partly broken down.

bullets: Photolysis in the thylakoids splits water using light energy, releasing oxygen
In the stroma, the Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide and builds it up into glucose
slides.heading: Photolysis splits water; the Calvin cycle fixes CO₂
slides.notes: Track two inputs separately: water in for photolysis and oxygen out, then carbon dioxide in for the Calvin cycle and glucose built up piece by piece.

bullets: Photosynthesis is capped by whichever factor - light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature - is in shortest supply
Raising a factor that is not limiting does nothing: only the shortest bar caps the rate
slides.heading: Photosynthesis is limited by the factor in shortest supply
slides.notes: Watch the carbon dioxide bar shrink and the rate cap with it. Close the loop: respiration never stops inside the plant - photosynthesis just masks it by day.

bullets: Aerobic respiration equation: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy, balanced as C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O
Complete aerobic breakdown yields about 32 ATP per glucose - far more than the anaerobic pathways in scene s4
slides.heading: Worked example: the aerobic respiration payoff
slides.notes: Talk through the equation atom by atom as in scene s2, then state the payoff from scene s3: about 32 ATP per glucose, rebuilt through the ATP-ADP cycle.

bullets: State the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast and in muscle, and explain why both yield far less ATP than aerobic respiration
Careful - a classmate says: Plants only respire at night. Correct them in one sentence, naming what plants do around the clock
slides.heading: Your turn: compare the pathways, then judge the claim
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the yeast and muscle products first, then on the exact sentence they used to correct the claim: Plants only respire at night.

bullets: On your own: write the aerobic respiration equation and state the ATP yield per glucose, then name the products of photolysis
Watch out for the trap one last time: Plants only respire at night. Say when plants respire, and why it looks switched off by day
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the balanced equation and about 32 ATP per glucose in your first answer, plus one clear around-the-clock respiration sentence in your second. Anyone repeating the claim Plants only respire at night. needs the trap scene again.
